canonicalExplanation.summary: `git fetch` **downloads** new commits from the remote and moves your **remote-tracking refs** (like `origin/main`) to match the server. It **never** touches your local branches or your working files, so it's always safe to run. After fetching, compare: `git status` says whether you're **ahead** (you have commits the server lacks), **behind** (the server has commits you lack) or **diverged** (both). `git log main..origin/main` lists what's new on the server; `git log origin/main..main` lists what's only yours. Then decide how to integrate.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner has been away for a day. They want to see what teammates pushed, but they're halfway through an edit and afraid `git pull` will mess up their files. After fetch, origin/main moves to the server's latest commit while local main and the learner's working files stay unchanged. In this lesson you'll fetch and explain ahead, behind and diverged states before integration.

```predict
{"question": "You have uncommitted edits and run git fetch. What happens to them?", "options": ["They may be overwritten", "Nothing: fetch only updates remote-tracking refs"], "answer": 1, "why": "Fetch is read-only for your branches and working tree."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Branches, merges and conflicts**, **Clone and remote configuration** and **Log, show and graph**.

sections.heading: The model: fetch moves origin/*, nothing else
sections.body:
```bash
git fetch origin
git status
#   Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged,
#   and have 1 and 3 different commits each, respectively.

git log --oneline main..origin/main    # the 3 new server commits.
git log --oneline origin/main..main    # my 1 local commit.
git diff main...origin/main            # what changed on the server since we split.
git log --oneline --graph --all -8     # see the fork.
```

| State | main..origin/main | origin/main..main |
|---|---|---|
| up to date. | empty. | empty. |
| behind. | commits. | empty. |
| ahead. | empty. | commits. |
| diverged. | commits. | commits. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why does git status sometimes say \"up to date\" when teammates have pushed?", "answer": "It compares with origin/main as of your last fetch. Without fetching, Git doesn't know about the new commits."}
```

examples.title: Checking what the team did
examples.situation: After fetch, origin/main moves to the server's latest commit while local main and the learner's working files stay unchanged.
walkthrough: **Fetch:** git fetch origin downloads three teammate commits.
**origin/main moves to the server's latest commit:** git log main..origin/main lists them.
**Local main and the learner's working files stay unchanged:** the half-finished edit is untouched; git status will report "behind by 3".
examples.result: The learner sees exactly what's new before deciding how to integrate.

examples.title: The diverged surprise
examples.situation: A learner committed locally, and a teammate pushed meanwhile. After fetch, status says diverged, 1 and 2.
walkthrough: origin/main..main shows the learner's one commit.
Integration will need a merge or rebase; the learner reviews the diff first.
examples.result: The learner integrates knowingly instead of being surprised by a merge.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Fetching is the same as pulling and can silently rewrite the current branch's files.
misconceptions.correction: Fetch only downloads objects and updates remote-tracking refs. Pull is fetch plus an integration step; only that second step changes your branch and files.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what happened to the uncommitted edits?

analogy.example: Fetching is like **checking the mailbox**: new letters (commits) arrive in the box (origin/main), but nothing on your desk (main, working tree) changes until you choose to open and file them.
limitations: Mail can pile up; so can commits, making later integration bigger.
Ahead means you have outgoing mail not yet posted.

nearTransfer.prompt: With two clones of a sandbox remote, create ahead, behind and diverged states in turn. After each, fetch, run git status, and show both log ranges.
scaffold: Push from one clone, commit in the other.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a short pre-integration checklist script that fetches, prints ahead/behind counts with git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main, and lists incoming commits. Test it in all three states.
scaffold: Never modify branches in the script.

remediation.explanation: Make it a habit: **fetch, then status, then read the incoming log** before any pull or merge.

recap.summary: To fetch and explain ahead, behind and diverged states, run git fetch to update remote-tracking refs without touching local branches or files, then compare main with origin/main using git status and the two log ranges, and inspect incoming changes before choosing how to integrate.
